Path
PATH
n. (rendering Hebrew 'ōrach, nāthīb, ma'gāl, and Greek tribos)
From Old English pæþ, common West Germanic, a track worn by feet. The Hebrew words all carry the same idea of a way made by going: 'ōrach is a well-trodden road, nāthīb a beaten track, and ma'gāl literally a wagon-rut or the circular track worn round an encampment. A path in Scripture is therefore not an abstract direction but a groove — something previous feet have cut and present feet fall into.

Biblical Definition

The path is Scripture's standing figure for the settled course of a life, and it is treated as a matter of direction, illumination, and inheritance rather than of momentary choice. The shepherd leads “in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake” (Psa 23:3) — the paths are already righteous before the sheep is in them, and the reason given is the shepherd's reputation rather than the sheep's merit. Illumination is by the word: “Thou wilt shew me the path of life” (Psa 16:11), a psalm the apostles apply directly to the resurrection of Christ, so that the path of life is first His and then, in Him, ours. Guidance is by submission rather than by insight: “In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths” (Pro 3:6), where the promise attaches to acknowledgment, not to cleverness. And because a path is a groove worn by previous travellers, the prophet's counsel is retrospective: “Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls” (Jer 6:16). The verse ends with the refusal that makes it a judgment oracle — But they said, We will not walk therein — and that refusal, not ignorance, is the usual reason men are lost. Scripture also speaks of paths that are crooked, of the path of the wicked which is as darkness, and of the just whose path is as the shining light that shineth more and more unto the perfect day.

Webster 1828 Definition

A track worn by the feet of those who have gone before; in Scripture the settled course of a life, led by the shepherd in righteousness, lighted by the word, directed by acknowledgment of God, and found by asking for the old paths rather than by devising new ones.

expand to see more

PATH, n. 1. A way beaten or trodden by the feet of man or beast; a track, or way formed by treading or walking.

2. Course of life; the manner in which a man walks. He leadeth me in the paths of righteousness. Psalm 23.

3. Course of providence, or of divine dealing. All the paths of the LORD are mercy and truth unto such as keep his covenant. Psalm 25.

4. Precepts; rule of conduct. Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path. Psalm 119.

5. The old paths; the ways of the fathers, and of the word of God, as distinguished from the new ways of men's devising. Jer. 6.

Key Scripture

Psalm 23:3 — "He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake."

Psalm 16:11 — "Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore."

Proverbs 3:6 — "In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths."

Jeremiah 6:16 — "Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein."

Modern Corruption

The path has been privatised: the biblical figure of a trodden way received from those who went before is replaced by the modern conviction that each man must find his own path, which is precisely the counsel Jer 6:16 records as refused.

expand to see more

The dominant modern usage of the word is self-referential — my path, your path, the path that is right for you — and it assumes that authenticity is the test and that a way received from others is by definition inauthentic. Scripture's figure runs the opposite direction. A path is worn by feet that came first; it is inherited, and its trustworthiness is established by where it has already led. Jeremiah's counsel is to stand, look, ask for the old paths, identify the good way among them, and then walk. Every verb in that sequence is an act of submission to something outside the self, and the promise attached is the one modern autonomy most conspicuously fails to deliver: ye shall find rest for your souls.

This is not a defence of mere traditionalism, and Jeremiah does not offer one. He does not say every old path is good; he says ask where the good way is among them, which requires discernment and a standard. The standard is the word, which is the lamp to the feet and the light to the path — near light for the next step and general light for the road. The Reformed instinct here is exactly right: the confessions and the fathers are consulted seriously as those who walked before us, and they are never authoritative over Scripture. What is refused is the notion that a man in his own generation, with his own lights, is competent to cut a new track through country he has never seen.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew has several words for a trodden way: 'ōrach (a well-worn road), nāthīb (a beaten track), and ma'gāl (a wagon rut or entrenchment). Greek tribos likewise names a way worn by rubbing and treading.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'ōrach (H734) — a way, path, road; used of the path of the just that shineth more and more (Pro 4:18) and of the paths of the LORD which are mercy and truth.

Hebrew nāthīb (H5410) — a beaten track; the word in Psa 119:105, a light unto my path, and in Job's question about the path no fowl knoweth.

Hebrew ma'gāl (H4570) — a wagon track, an entrenchment, a rut; the paths of righteousness of Psa 23:3 and the paths of Pro 4:26, ponder the path of thy feet.

Hebrew derek (H1870) — way, road, manner of life; the broader term standing behind the two ways of Psa 1 and the good way of Jer 6:16.

Greek tribos (G5147) — a worn path, a beaten way; used in the Baptist's summons, make his paths straight (Mat 3:3), quoting Isa 40:3.

Usage

"Of the course in which God leads: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness (Psa 23:3); all the paths of the LORD are mercy and truth (Psa 25:10)."

"Of guidance and illumination: he shall direct thy paths (Pro 3:6); a light unto my path (Psa 119:105); thou wilt shew me the path of life (Psa 16:11)."

"Of the inherited way and its refusal: ask for the old paths (Jer 6:16); the path of the just is as the shining light (Pro 4:18); the way of the wicked is as darkness (Pro 4:19)."
